Season 3 · Episode 14 Released Tuesday, June 17, 2026

Building a tool library from a single donated drill.

A conversation with Marcus Haines, founder of Foundry Row

Duration 1 hr 12 min
Recorded May 28, 2026
Episode no. S03E14
Location Oakland · the garage
15:53 1:12:14
Or listen in Apple Podcasts Spotify Overcast Pocket Casts RSS

Marcus Haines spent four years turning a rented Oakland garage into a tool-lending nonprofit that now serves four East Bay neighborhoods. We talk about the slow, mostly unphotogenic work of building public infrastructure when nobody asked for it — and about the suggestion from a single member, posted in the comments of a Patreon update, that ended up quietly reshaping the entire membership model.

About the guest

Marcus Haines

Founder & Director · Foundry Row · Oakland, CA

Marcus is the founder of Foundry Row, a free, member-supported tool library now serving the Fruitvale, San Antonio, Dimond, and Eastmont neighborhoods of East Oakland. The collection began in 2021 with a single donated DeWalt drill and a chest freezer's worth of secondhand hand tools. It now circulates over 2,400 items — power tools, garden equipment, sewing machines, ladders, a 12-inch table saw, and one large, beloved pasta maker — to roughly 3,700 members across four storefronts.

Before Foundry Row, Marcus spent twelve years as a journeyman carpenter and another four running the cabinet shop for a custom millwork outfit in Berkeley. He is a 2024 fellow of the Just Transition civic infrastructure cohort and has written about the cooperative-tool-library model for The Long Now Quarterly and Shareable.

Show notes

Mentioned in the conversation. Compiled by Priya Anand-Kowalski with help, as always, from the listeners who emailed corrections.

  • 00:00 Cold open: Marcus reading the original Craigslist post he wrote in February 2021 looking for "any unwanted tools in working condition" — the post that launched the whole thing.
  • 04:18 Foundry Row's public catalog and reservation system — open source, built by a volunteer named Theo who lives in Detroit and has, at the time of recording, never met Marcus in person.
  • 11:42 The Tools We Need by Hellen Lawrence Quattro (Long Reach Press, 2019) — a small book about the politics of tool ownership that Marcus has bought and given away "probably forty copies of by now."
  • 19:05 The North Portland Tool Library, which Marcus visited in 2020 and credits as the model that proved this could work in an American city without university funding.
  • 26:40 Tools as Infrastructure — Marcus's 2023 essay in Shareable, the piece that ended up bringing in their first $50,000 unrestricted grant from a small family foundation in Berkeley.
  • 34:11 The Eastmont Mall pop-up branch, the second-newest of Foundry Row's four locations, opened in March 2025 in a former Sears auto-service bay.
  • 42:28 "The suggestion that changed everything" — the original Patreon comment from a member named Diana, posted October 14, 2023, suggesting Foundry Row let members opt into a small monthly contribution instead of charging a flat membership fee. Quoted in full in the transcript.
  • 51:14 The Library Book by Susan Orlean — the book that, Marcus says, gave him "language for the kind of institution I didn't realize I was building."
  • 58:30 The East Bay Cooperative Federation, the small umbrella org that helped Foundry Row incorporate as a 501(c)(3) in 2022 — and which now provides shared back-office services to fourteen Bay Area cooperatives.
  • 1:04:55 Marcus's three "what I'd tell someone starting today" recommendations — read in full at the timestamp.
  • 1:09:20 How to become a Foundry Row member (free, two-page form, $5/mo opt-in contribution if you want).

MARCUS: No. I didn't even know it was a tool library. CASSIA: When did the name come?

MARCUS: About a month later. I had a friend, Renata — different Renata than the one on the previous episode — and she sent me a link to the North Portland Tool Library. And I clicked it and I just sat at my kitchen table for, I want to say, an hour. Because I had been doing this thing in my head where I thought I was inventing something. CASSIA: 11:30Can we — for anyone listening who has genuinely never used or seen one — what is a tool library? Just, the simplest version.

MARCUS: Yeah. So. The simplest version. Imagine a regular library. You walk in. There's a desk, there's a person at the desk, there's stuff on shelves. The stuff on the shelves is not books, it's tools. You take a tool home for a week. You bring it back. If you broke it, you tell us, we figure it out together. That's it. That's the whole thing.

CASSIA: And it's free.

MARCUS: It's free. Membership is free. Borrowing is free. Late fees — we tried late fees for the first eight months and we got rid of them. They were doing the opposite of what we wanted them to do. They were keeping people away who'd had a bad experience with a tool, instead of bringing the tool back.

CASSIA: So no late fees, no charges, no —

MARCUS: No charges of any kind. We ask for a contribution if you can. We do not ask for the contribution at the front desk. We send you an email a month after you join and we say, "Hey, the library cost about four dollars to lend you that drill — here's our budget if you want to see it, here's how you can chip in if you want." That's it. We never bring it up again unless you ask.

CASSIA: That's so — that's a very specific posture. Where did that come from?

MARCUS: Honestly? My mom. My mom worked at the public library in Modesto for thirty-one years. And she was very clear, my whole childhood, that a library is something that you do not make people prove they deserve. You just — they walk in, and you trust them. And if 5% of them don't return what they took, that is a price you pay willingly, because the alternative is that the other 95% feel surveilled. And the surveilled feeling — she would tell me this — the surveilled feeling is what kills a library.

CASSIA: 17:14That's a beautiful idea. That's a — okay. So you have the drill, you have the toaster oven, you have a name. When does it become a thing you can walk into?

MARCUS: June 2021. So about four months after the Craigslist post. By then I had about — I want to say two hundred and thirty tools? In my garage. And the garage was full. Like, I could not park my car in there anymore. My downstairs neighbor was being unbelievably gracious about the fact that there was a circular saw on the staircase. CASSIA: The Fruitvale storefront. Tell me about finding that.

MARCUS: So. The Fruitvale storefront. 19:12That place is on International Boulevard, between 35th and 36th, and it had been a check-cashing place that closed in 2019. It had sat empty for two years. The landlord, who I will not name on the air but who I love very much —

CASSIA: [laughs]

MARCUS: — he agreed to rent it to me for nine hundred dollars a month, which in Oakland in 2021 was bananas, and he agreed to it because I told him exactly what I was going to do with it, and he said, and I quote, "Okay, but I'm telling you right now, the neighborhood doesn't need this." And I said, "I think it does." And he said, "Well, we'll see." And it took about six months for me to be able to look him in the eye and not feel like he was right.

CASSIA: What did the first six months look like?

MARCUS: Very slow. Like, painfully slow. I would open the doors at ten in the morning on a Saturday and I would sit at a folding table with a clipboard, and on a good day, three people would come in. Sometimes the three people were the same person three times. And I thought — there was a period of maybe four months in there where I genuinely thought I had made a very expensive mistake.

CASSIA: What changed?

MARCUS: A guy named Hector came in. 23:40And Hector — this is a story I tell a lot, I'm sorry if anyone's heard it. Hector was a retired auto-body guy. Lived two blocks away. He came in, he looked around for forty minutes, didn't say anything. And then he came up to the desk and he said, "You need a sign." And I said, "I have a sign." And he pointed out the window and he said, "That is not a sign. That is a piece of paper taped to a window. I am going to bring you a sign."

CASSIA: And he did.

MARCUS: The next Tuesday. Hand-painted. Wood. Said FOUNDRY ROW · TOOLS FOR THE NEIGHBORHOOD. And after that sign went up, the number of people walking in went from three a day to about fifteen. Not because the sign was that good — the sign was great, but it wasn't, like, magic. It was because Hector then went to every business on a four-block stretch of International and personally told them about it. He'd been living there for thirty years. He had a credibility I did not yet have, and he gave it to me. For free. Just gave it to me.

CASSIA: 26:40I read your Shareable piece — the one from 2023. And there's a line in it that I underlined and I want to read it back to you. You wrote: "The work of building public infrastructure when nobody asked for it is the work of waiting to be asked." Did you know what you meant when you wrote that?

MARCUS: [long pause] I think I knew what I felt. I'm not sure I knew what I meant. Can I — can I think about that for a second?

CASSIA: Please.

MARCUS: [pause] I think — okay. I think what I was trying to say is that there's this — there's a certain kind of building, like the kind that gets covered in business magazines, where you have an idea and you go and you announce it and you put it on a website and you raise money and you hire people and you ship it. And that is a real way to build a thing, I'm not knocking it. But there's another kind of building, where what you are actually doing is making yourself available. You are saying — I am here, this thing exists, when you decide you want it, it will be ready for you. And the building is not the launching of it. The building is the staying. The building is the four months of three-people-a-day, where what you are doing is proving to the neighborhood that you will still be here in a year.

CASSIA: The staying.

MARCUS: The staying is the work. I think I really do believe that now. I'm not sure I believed it then. Then I just thought I was failing.

CASSIA: You said earlier — there was a member who never came back. Can you tell me about that?

CASSIA: And she never came back.

MARCUS: She never came back. I tried to find her. I asked around. The guy who worked the desk that day is no longer with us. And the policy — the ID policy — is gone. We do not ask for ID anymore. We ask for an email or a phone number, and if you don't have those, we ask for the name of any neighbor who can vouch for you. That's it. That whole change of policy is because of Marisol. CASSIA: [pause] Thank you for telling me that.

MARCUS: Yeah.

CASSIA: 34:22Let's — can we move into the 501(c)(3) stuff? Because I know that took a long time, and I think a lot of people listening have wanted to start something nonprofit-shaped and have been chased off by the paperwork.

MARCUS: Eighteen months. Eighteen months. And the reason was — okay, this is a deeply unsexy story, but the reason is that I tried to do it myself, and then I tried to do it with the wrong lawyer, and then I tried to do it with a free legal clinic that was overwhelmed, and then I finally — finally — found the East Bay Cooperative Federation, who I cannot say enough nice things about. They had a template. They had walked, at that point, eleven other small Bay Area co-ops and nonprofits through the exact same process. They charged me on a sliding scale. They got us our 501(c)(3) determination letter in five and a half months.

CASSIA: Five and a half months versus eighteen months trying to do it alone.

MARCUS: Yes. And the lesson — if I have one lesson from all of this — is, you do not have to figure out the legal structure by yourself. Find the people who have done it for organizations that look like yours, and pay them whatever you can pay them. It is the best money you will ever spend.

CASSIA: What did the 501(c)(3) actually unlock?

MARCUS: Two things. One, the obvious — bigger donations become tax-deductible, which means people who care about tax deductions, which is a real demographic of donor, can now give us money. The second thing, which is way bigger and nobody talks about, is — landlords. Landlords will rent to a 501(c)(3) at rates and on terms that they will not give to a guy with a Craigslist post. Our second location, our third location, our fourth location — all of those leases are at below-market rent because the landlords get a piece of paper they can point to for their own community-investment portfolio. The legal status is, like, half the reason we have four locations now.

CASSIA: Huh.

MARCUS: That is the unsexiest possible answer to the question of how we grew, and it is the true one.

CASSIA: 42:28Okay. I want to talk about the membership model. Because I think this is the single most interesting thing about Foundry Row, and I think it is — it is what I want every nonprofit listening to this to hear. Tell me about Diana's comment.

MARCUS: Diana. [pause] Okay. So. By October 2023 we'd been operating for about two and a half years. We had a flat-rate membership — five dollars a month, you got the library card, that was the deal. We had about nine hundred members. The five-dollar-a-month was — for a lot of people, that was fine, that was a coffee, no problem. For a meaningful number of people, that was the reason they didn't sign up. We knew that. We had data on it. We were stuck on what to do about it.

CASSIA: And Diana —

MARCUS: Diana posted a comment on one of our Patreon updates. October 14th, 2023. I have it in front of me actually. She wrote — can I read it?

CASSIA: Please.

MARCUS: She wrote: "I love this place. I would pay twenty dollars a month if I could. I do not understand why you charge five dollars instead of letting me, and the people who can afford it, pay more so that the people who can't afford five dollars don't have to pay anything. Just — let me pay what I want. Let everybody pay what they want. Show us the budget. Trust us." That was the comment.

CASSIA: That's the whole comment?

MARCUS: That's the whole comment. And I read it on my phone, in line at a Trader Joe's. And I stood there for probably ninety seconds just staring at it. Because — every nonprofit consultant I had ever talked to, every funding workshop I'd been to, every Stanford-MBA-pro-bono advisor — every single one of them had told me, you need a clear, simple, predictable membership fee. Five dollars. Ten dollars. Pick a number, defend it, never change it. And Diana, who has, like, no nonprofit experience that I know of, in a Patreon comment, in two paragraphs — she said the opposite, and she was right, and she was right in a way that took me about four months to figure out how to actually implement.

CASSIA: What did you do?

MARCUS: 47:18We made it free. Everything. Membership, borrowing, all of it, free. We removed the five-dollar fee in February 2024. And the only thing we added was — when you sign up, on the welcome email, we say, "The library cost about $X to operate last month per active member. Here's our full budget, line by line. If you want to chip in, here's a sliding scale of $1, $3, $5, $10, $25 a month. If you don't want to chip in, that is genuinely fine, we are glad you are here, please use the library." That's it.

CASSIA: And what happened?

MARCUS: Our monthly recurring revenue went up by 41% in three months. And our membership doubled in eight months. Both. At the same time. We are now — we are now bringing in more money, per member, on average, than we were before, because the people who were giving five dollars are now giving ten or fifteen or in some cases — Diana is giving twenty-five — and the people who weren't giving anything are now members and are also, a lot of them, kicking in a couple of dollars when they can.

CASSIA: So everyone wins.

MARCUS: Everyone wins. And I would never have done it without Diana. I sent her a long email after we made the change. I told her, you reshaped my organization. She wrote back, and she said — and this is the part that I think about all the time — she said, "I'm a librarian. This is just how public libraries work."

CASSIA: [laughs] Oh, of course she's a librarian.

MARCUS: Of course she is. Of course she is. The whole thing was already invented. I just hadn't been listening to librarians.

CASSIA: 51:14Marcus, can I ask you about the hard part?

MARCUS: Sure.

CASSIA: You mentioned, before we started recording, that there was a week in 2024 where you almost shut the whole thing down.

MARCUS: [long pause] Yeah. Okay. I — yeah. Can I — can I take a sip of coffee? [pause] Okay. So. November 2024. We had just opened the Eastmont location. We had just hired our second full-time employee. We were about to lose our biggest grant — they had a leadership transition and they shifted their giving priorities away from local infrastructure. I had not slept more than five hours a night for about four weeks. And my dad — my dad had a stroke. In Modesto. And I — I drove down to be with him, and I sat in the hospital, and I just — I was just done. I called my board chair from the hospital cafeteria and I said, I think I have to step back. I think I can't do this. I think I'm going to wind it down.

CASSIA: [quietly] What did she say?

MARCUS: She said — her name is Renee — she said, "Marcus, you are exhausted and your dad is in the hospital. You are not allowed to make that decision today. We will talk about it in six weeks. In the meantime I am going to tell the staff what is going on, and I am going to ask the volunteers to keep things running for a month, and you are going to take care of your dad." And she — she did it. She did all of it. I didn't open my laptop for thirty-one days. And the library kept running. Without me. Because we had — we had quietly built a thing that was bigger than just me, and I had not noticed.

CASSIA: And your dad?

MARCUS: He's good. He's — he's slower than he was. He's still in Modesto. I see him every other weekend now. He's — he's the one who actually came up with the name Foundry Row, did I ever tell you that?

CASSIA: No, you didn't.

MARCUS: Yeah. Foundry Row was a real place. It was — there used to be a stretch of the rail line in West Oakland, in the forties and fifties, that was all small metal-casting shops. Family-owned, mostly. Working-class. They poured the iron grates that are still in half the storm drains in this city. My dad's family knew people who worked there. And when I was looking for a name, in 2021, I called him, and he said — without missing a beat — he said, Foundry Row. He said, your great-uncle worked on Foundry Row. He said, that's a place that made things for the city. And I thought — that's the name. Done.

CASSIA: [pause] Marcus, that's beautiful.

MARCUS: Yeah.

CASSIA: Can I push back on one thing, though?

MARCUS: Please.

CASSIA: 56:48When you tell the story of almost shutting down — and I love that you told me — but the takeaway you offered is, "we'd quietly built a thing that was bigger than me." And I — I love that. But I think there's a version of that takeaway that lets the founder off the hook a little. That lets you not look at why you almost burned out. And I'm curious if — three years later, eighteen months later — do you think there were structural things you should have changed earlier? About how you were running yourself?

MARCUS: [long pause] Yeah. Yes. The honest answer is yes. I should have hired a second full-time person a year earlier than I did. I should have built a board that was more than three people, three years ago. I should have — I should have had a written sick-leave policy for myself. I did not. I had one for everyone else. And the reason I didn't is that I had this — I think a lot of founders have this — this feeling that the thing only works if I'm the one doing it. And that is, like, the founder's curse. That is the thing you have to walk yourself out of. And I had not done that work. November 2024 was, partly, the bill for not having done that work.

CASSIA: Thank you for that.

MARCUS: Yeah. Yeah, no, it's a fair pushback.

CASSIA: 58:30Tell me about working with the other co-ops. The East Bay Cooperative Federation, the bookstore folks, the bakery folks. What's that ecosystem like?

MARCUS: It's the best part of the job, honestly. There are now about fourteen small worker-owned or community-owned organizations in the East Bay that share a back office — the Federation runs our bookkeeping, our HR, our compliance, our payroll. We pay them a flat percentage of our budget. It's the single biggest reason we can operate with two and a half employees instead of needing five. And once you're in that network, the lateral relationships are — they're the thing.

CASSIA: What does that look like, day to day?

MARCUS: It looks like, the bakery had a freezer go down last winter and Sage texted me at six in the morning and said, "Do you have a spare freezer?" And we did, because somebody had donated a chest freezer the month before, and I drove it over before opening. It looks like — the Foxglove bookstore is doing a community-fundraiser event next month and they asked if we could lend them ten folding chairs. Of course. It looks like, when the Federation gets a grant, they parcel out the unrestricted portion across all fourteen of us. It is — it is mutual aid in a very practical form.

CASSIA: Is there anything you don't share?

MARCUS: [laughs] Email lists. We do not share email lists. That is the one line. You earn your own list. You do not get to borrow somebody else's list. Otherwise, basically everything.

CASSIA: 1:04:55If somebody is listening to this — and I know they are — and they are thinking, I want to start a tool library, or I want to start something like a tool library, in their city, in their town — what would you tell them?

MARCUS: Three things. Can I just go through three things?

CASSIA: Please.

MARCUS: One. Do not start by raising money. Do not write a grant proposal. Do not file paperwork. Start by getting one tool from one neighbor and lending it to one other neighbor. If you cannot do that, you cannot do this. If you can do that, you have already done the hardest part. Everything else is logistics.

MARCUS: Two. Find the people who have already done what you are trying to do. Call them. They will pick up. I cold-emailed the woman who runs the North Portland Tool Library in 2021 and she got on a Zoom with me within a week. The cooperative-tool-library world is small and generous and they will help you, for free, immediately. Do not try to invent anything. Use what's been built.

MARCUS: Three. Be willing to stay. The whole thing is the staying. I said that earlier and I keep saying it because I keep believing it more. There is no shortcut to legitimacy in a neighborhood. You have to be the place that is still there in a year. So if you don't think you can be still there in a year, do something else, build something else. But if you can — if you can promise yourself you will still be opening the doors in a year, in two years, in five — then start. Then absolutely start.

CASSIA: 1:09:20Marcus, last question. Or — second to last, actually. What does success look like to you, six years from now?

MARCUS: Six years from now. Six years from now, I want Foundry Row to be in every neighborhood in Oakland that wants one. I do not want to be the founder of any of those branches. I want to have trained the people who founded them. I want to be — I want to be the guy who answers their cold emails. I want to be the version of the North Portland Tool Library woman who got on a Zoom with me. That's the success. The success is not me running fourteen branches. The success is me running zero branches and being one phone call away from fourteen branches that are running themselves.

CASSIA: And the actual last question. What are you reading right now?

MARCUS: [laughs] 1:11:08I'm reading A Paradise Built in Hell by Rebecca Solnit. For the third time. It's the book I go back to when I get tired. Solnit's whole argument is — when disaster strikes, the thing that emerges is not chaos, it's mutual aid. It's neighbors taking care of neighbors. It's the part of us that we have been trained to forget about. I find it — I find it very useful to be reminded of that, a lot.

CASSIA: Marcus Haines, thank you so much for doing this.

MARCUS: Cassia, thank you. Thank you for having me. Thank you for the show. I — I listen every Tuesday. It means a lot to be on it.

CASSIA: 1:12:00Foundry Row is at foundryrow.org. Four locations across East Oakland. If you've got a tool in a closet that hasn't been used in a year, you know where to take it. We'll be back next Tuesday with the wonderful Naomi Estefan-Brooke, who runs a small community-supported fishery out of Half Moon Bay. Until then — take care of each other.
